name: Ilam
tagline: Nepal's oldest tea hills, rolled green to the Indian border
meta_description: Ilam, eastern Nepal: tea gardens dated to 1863, Mai Pokhari wetland, akabare chilli and misty ridges. How to reach, where to stay, what to do.
summary: Ilam is the hill town at the heart of Nepal's tea country, about 1,300 m up in the far east. Tea has grown here since the 1860s. Come for the garden walks, the morning mist, the Mai Pokhari wetland and a slow two or three days among Limbu, Rai and Lepcha villages.
intro: Ilam bazaar sits on a ridge of the Mahabharat hills, a three to four hour drive up the Mechi Highway from the Terai plains of Jhapa. The town is small: one long main road, a few chowks, a college, tea shops that sell loose leaf by the hundred grams. The tea gardens begin at the edge of the bazaar and run downhill in clipped green rows, with pickers in the bushes from late March to November.

Most people who come here are Nepali and Indian families on a weekend from the plains, and on Saturdays the viewpoints and tea shops fill up. Fewer foreigners make the trip, which is part of the pleasure. On a weekday you can walk out of your guesthouse into the Ilam Tea Estate before breakfast, watch the mist (kuhiro) burn off the slopes, and be the only visitor in the rows, with nothing but the pickers' voices and the bells of the cattle below.

Ilam works as a base for the wider tea country: Kanyam and Fikkal to the south-east, Mai Pokhari and the long road to Sandakpur to the north, and the villages of cardamom and ginger farmers in between. Give it two nights at least. A third lets you add a farm visit, a walk to a cardamom plot, a homestay night, or a day on the ridge with nothing to do but drink tea and watch the cloud move through the valleys.

story.title: A tea town on the Darjeeling side of the hills
paras: Ilam bazaar was set up in 1818 as the seat of the Ilam gauda, the administrative post the Gorkhali state used to govern this far corner of the new kingdom. Before that, the hills belonged to the Limbu chiefs of Limbuwan, whose traditional territories stretched east of the Arun to the Mechi river on the Sikkim and Darjeeling border. Many of the old Limbu place names survive in the villages around town, and Limbu families still farm the slopes their ancestors held.

Tea came in the 1860s. Ilam's tea history is usually dated to 1863, and a factory followed a few years later. The hills here share their soil, slope and mist with Darjeeling across the border, and for much of the 20th century green leaf from Nepal's estates was sold over the border to Indian factories. Nepal set up its own Tea Development Corporation in 1966, and private estates and smallholders took a larger share after the National Tea Policy of 2000.

Today Ilam and neighbouring Jhapa grow most of Nepal's tea, with Ilam known for orthodox hill leaf, alongside cardamom, ginger, broom grass, potatoes and the tiny round akabare chilli. People here speak of Ilam's six A's: alu (potato), alain (milk), alainchi (cardamom), aduwa (ginger), amriso (broom grass) and akabare. In 2010 Ilam became the first municipality in Nepal to ban plastic bags in its market, a point of pride you will hear about in the tea shops along the main road.

legend: A story told in Ilam's tea shops says the first tea bushes in Nepal grew from seeds the Chinese emperor sent as a gift to Prime Minister Jung Bahadur Rana, and that some of those seedlings were carried east and planted on these slopes. Historians argue about the details, and some point instead to plants and know-how from Darjeeling next door. Locals tell it either way with a smile and a refill.
people: Ilam is mixed. Limbu (Yakthung) families have the oldest roots here, with Rai, Brahmin, Chhetri, Newar, Magar, Gurung, Tamang and Sherpa households alongside. Ilam district is also home to most of Nepal's small Lepcha (Rong) community. Tea work, dairy, cardamom and ginger keep the villages going, and many families have a son or daughter working abroad. Nepali is the common language; Limbu is spoken in many homes.

untold.fact: Ilam bazaar was established in 1818 as the headquarters of the Ilam gauda, an administrative post of the Gorkhali state, more than forty years before tea was planted here.
In 2010 Ilam municipality became the first in Nepal to ban plastic bags from its market, an early local step that other towns later followed. Shopkeepers in the bazaar still mention it with pride.
Mai Pokhari, a small lake and wetland at about 2,100 m north of Ilam bazaar, was designated a Ramsar wetland of international importance in October 2008.

taste.name: Akabare khursani achar
taste.text: A pickle of Ilam's small, round, very hot akabare chilli, often mixed with lemon, mustard oil and timur pepper. Every kitchen in town makes its own. Ask for it with dal bhat at any bhojanalaya on the main road, and buy a jar in the bazaar to take home.

highlights.title: Ilam Tea Estate at first light
highlights.text: The old estate starts where the bazaar ends. Walk the paths between the rows at 6 am, when the pickers arrive and mist hangs in the valley below. The garden is a working estate, so keep to the paths and ask before photographing the pickers.

highlights.title: Mai Pokhari wetland
highlights.text: A small, sacred lake at about 2,100 m, surrounded by forest and listed as a Ramsar wetland since 2008. Hindu and Buddhist pilgrims both come here. It is roughly 1.5–2 hours by jeep from Ilam bazaar on a rough road.

highlights.title: Tea tasting in the bazaar
highlights.text: Shops along the main road sell orthodox Ilam tea by weight: first flush from late March, second flush from May, autumn flush in October–November. Ask to taste two or three side by side before you buy.

highlights.title: Ridge walks above town
highlights.text: Footpaths leave the bazaar in every direction, past cardamom plots, cowsheds and terraced maize. A half-day loop with a local guide shows how a hill farm in Ilam actually works, from milking and fodder cutting to ginger and broom grass.

highlights.title: A base for the tea country
highlights.text: From Ilam you can reach Kanyam and Fikkal in about 1.5 hours, Mai Pokhari in 2, and the Sandakpur ridge in a long jeep day. Two or three nights here cover the best of it without rushing.

how_to_reach.text: Fly Kathmandu to Bhadrapur (about 45–50 minutes, several flights a day in season). From Bhadrapur it is roughly 100 km and 3–4 hours by car to Ilam via Birtamod or Charali and the Mechi Highway. Flight schedules change by season; check current status before you travel.

Overnight buses run from Kathmandu to Ilam, about 600 km and 14–16 hours via the East–West Highway. A private car takes two days if you stop on the way. From the Terai, the Mechi Highway climbs 74 km from the East–West Highway to Ilam bazaar.

where_to_stay: Ilam bazaar has simple hotels and family guesthouses along the main road and near the tea estate; expect clean rooms, hot water by geyser or bucket, and dal bhat downstairs. Several homestays operate in the villages around town and in the tea gardens, where you sleep in a family house and eat what they eat. There are no international chain hotels in Ilam. We book rooms that we have checked recently, close enough to the estate to walk in at dawn.
tips: Bring a warm layer even in May; evenings at 1,300 m are cool and the mist can be damp.
The tea estates are working farms, so ask before photographing pickers and do not pick leaves.
Buy tea in small packs from two or three shops and compare; prices and quality vary more than labels suggest.
Saturdays and Nepali holidays bring families up from the Terai, so book rooms ahead for those dates.
Carry cash in Nepali rupees; ATMs exist in the bazaar but can run dry on holiday weekends.

experiences.title: Dawn walk through Ilam Tea Estate
experiences.summary: A quiet early walk through the old tea estate at the edge of Ilam bazaar, timed for the pickers arriving and the mist lifting off the valley. Our guide explains plucking, flushes and how green leaf becomes orthodox tea.
body: We meet at your guesthouse at about 6 am and walk five minutes downhill into the estate. The rows here are old, clipped to waist height, and laid along the contour so you can follow them like terraces, with shade trees standing over the bushes at intervals. On most mornings in spring and autumn a layer of kuhiro sits in the valley below, and the far ridges float on top of it. Our guide picks a route that keeps you on the main paths and away from areas being sprayed or pruned.

Pickers, almost all women, arrive around seven with baskets on their backs held by a namlo, the cloth strap across the forehead. Our guide explains the rule they work by, two leaves and a bud, and why the first flush in late March and April sells for more than the monsoon leaf. You learn how the day's leaf is weighed, how pickers are paid, and where it goes next. If the women are willing, you can try plucking for a few minutes under their eye.

We finish at a tea shop in the bazaar with two or three cups side by side: a light first or second flush, a darker autumn tea, and perhaps a green. It is the simplest way to learn what you like before you buy, and the shopkeepers enjoy the questions. Breakfast follows at a local eatery or back at your guesthouse, and you have the rest of the day free for Kanyam, Mai Pokhari or simply a slow afternoon in town.

faqs.q: Do I need a ticket to walk in Ilam Tea Estate?
faqs.a: On our last visits there was no ticket to walk the main paths through the estate next to the bazaar, though rules can change and some private gardens charge a small fee or ask you to stay out. Keep to the paths, do not pick leaves, and ask before photographing the pickers. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When do pickers work in Ilam?
faqs.a: Plucking runs from about late March to November, starting with the first flush in spring and finishing with the autumn flush in October and November. Pickers usually start in the early morning. In December to February the bushes rest, so you see pruned rows and very little work, though the walks are still pleasant.

faqs.q: Is the dawn walk hard?
faqs.a: No. It is a gentle walk of 2–3 km on estate paths with some short ups and downs, at about 1,300 m. Wear shoes with grip, because the clay paths can be slippery when the mist is heavy, and bring a light jacket for the first hour.

experiences.title: Mai Pokhari wetland day trip
experiences.summary: A jeep trip north of Ilam to Mai Pokhari, a small sacred lake at about 2,100 m inside forest. It is a Ramsar-listed wetland and a pilgrimage site for both Hindus and Buddhists, with a short walk around the shore.
body: Mai Pokhari lies north of Ilam bazaar, roughly 1.5–2 hours by jeep on a road that climbs through tea, cardamom and then mixed forest of oak, rhododendron and bamboo. The lake itself is small, with a temple on its shore and prayer flags strung through the trees. It was listed as a Ramsar wetland in 2008, protected for its bog plants, birds and amphibians, and it sits at about 2,100 m, so the air is noticeably cooler than in town.

Pilgrims come throughout the year, and in larger numbers on full-moon and festival days. Hindus treat the lake as a form of the goddess, and Buddhist visitors walk around it clockwise, spinning prayer wheels and leaving offerings. Our guide tells you the local beliefs about the lake, shows you where offerings are left, and explains the simple rules visitors follow: no swimming, no fishing, no rubbish in the water, and quiet near the shrine.

The walk around the shore takes about 45 minutes on a forest path, with benches and viewpoints along the way. Birdwatchers should bring binoculars; the forest is good for small hill birds in the early hours. In spring the rhododendrons are out on the slopes above. We pack a lunch or eat at a simple bhojanalaya by the car park, then drive back to Ilam in the afternoon, stopping at a tea garden on the way.

faqs.q: How far is Mai Pokhari from Ilam?
faqs.a: Mai Pokhari is roughly 1.5–2 hours by jeep north of Ilam bazaar, on a partly rough road that climbs to about 2,100 m. Most people do it as a day trip and return to Ilam for the night. In the monsoon the road can be slow or blocked by landslides, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Mai Pokhari?
faqs.a: There has been a small entry fee collected locally for visitors to the lake area at times. Amounts and rules change, so carry small Nepali rupee notes and ask our guide on the day. Pilgrims visiting the temple usually make their own offerings.

faqs.q: What should I wear at Mai Pokhari?
faqs.a: Bring a warm layer and a rain jacket; at about 2,100 m it is several degrees colder than Ilam and often misty. The lake is a sacred site, so dress modestly, walk around it clockwise and do not swim or throw anything into the water.

experiences.title: Farm day and homestay night near Ilam
experiences.summary: A night with a farming family in the hills around Ilam: milking time, a walk to the cardamom and ginger plots, an evening meal cooked on a wood stove, and a morning cup of tea grown a few metres from the door.
body: Ilam's economy is not only tea. Most families also keep a cow or two, grow large cardamom under the shade of alder trees, dig ginger and cut amriso, the broom grass sold across Nepal. Milk from these villages goes to the dairies that make Ilam's cheese and chhurpi. A night in a village homestay shows you how these crops fit together through the year, and how a family keeps several small incomes going at once.

We drive or walk from the bazaar to the village in the afternoon. Your host takes you round the farm, explains how cardamom pods are dried over a wood fire in a small kiln called a bhatti, and lets you help with whatever needs doing, whether that is cutting fodder or bringing the cows in. Dinner is usually rice, dal, a green, a pickle with akabare chilli, and perhaps chicken; tell us in advance if you do not eat meat.

Rooms are simple and clean, usually with two beds, thick quilts and a window onto the fields, and shared toilets in most houses. Evenings are early: families eat around seven and sleep soon after. In the morning there is tea from the family's own bushes or from the nearest garden, a breakfast of roti or puffed rice, and then we walk back to Ilam or carry on to Kanyam. We pay the family directly for your stay and meals.

faqs.q: What is a homestay near Ilam like?
faqs.a: You sleep in a family's house, usually in a simple room with two beds and blankets, and share their meals. Toilets are often outside and shared. Hosts speak some Nepali and a little English; our guide translates. It is comfortable but basic, and the point is the family, the farm and the food.

faqs.q: When is cardamom harvested in Ilam?
faqs.a: Large cardamom is usually harvested from about September to November, and the pods are then dried over a wood fire. October and November are the best months to see harvesting and drying. Ginger is dug at about the same time of year.

faqs.q: Can vegetarians stay in an Ilam homestay?
faqs.a: Yes. Dal bhat, vegetables, pickles and milk tea are vegetarian anyway, and hosts are used to guests who do not eat meat. Tell us when you book so we can tell the family, and mention any allergies too, especially to chilli, nuts or dairy, which are common in local cooking.

experiences.title: Tea tasting in Ilam bazaar
experiences.summary: A tasting of orthodox Ilam teas across flushes and styles in the bazaar's tea shops, with a guide who explains grades, how to brew them and what a fair price looks like before you buy.
body: Ilam's main road has several shops selling loose orthodox tea, plus packets from the estates and smallholder cooperatives that buy leaf from village growers. Most will brew a few cups if you ask, using small porcelain sets and timers. With our guide we taste three to five teas side by side and talk through what you are drinking: colour, smell, body and the dry feeling some teas leave on the tongue.

First flush, picked from late March, is light and pale. Second flush, from May, is fuller. Autumn flush in October and November is darker and rounder. You will also find green and white teas, and the strong CTC tea most Nepali households boil with milk and sugar. Each has its own brewing time and water temperature, and we show you both, so you can get the same cup at home with an ordinary kettle.

There is no pressure to buy, and we suggest small packs from more than one shop so you can compare at home. Ilam tea is still far cheaper here than in Kathmandu or abroad, and the shopkeepers will vacuum-pack it for your bag. If you find a tea you love, ask which garden or cooperative it came from; many smallholder teas are sold under a shop's own name, and the shopkeeper usually knows the grower.

faqs.q: How much does Ilam tea cost in the bazaar?
faqs.a: Prices vary a lot by flush and grade. Everyday CTC tea is cheap, while good orthodox first flush or specialty green costs several times more per 100 grams. Ask for a price per 100 grams in each shop, taste before you buy, and compare two or three shops before choosing.

faqs.q: Can I take Ilam tea home on a flight?
faqs.a: Yes, dry packed tea is normally allowed in checked and hand luggage on flights from Nepal. Ask the shop to vacuum-pack it so it stays fresh and does not crush. Customs rules for food and plant products differ by country, so check your own country's limits before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the difference between orthodox and CTC tea?
faqs.a: Orthodox tea is rolled whole leaf, brewed light without milk, and comes in flushes through the season. CTC (crush, tear, curl) tea is cut into small granules for a strong, quick brew, which is what most Nepalis boil with milk and sugar as chiya. Ilam makes both.

faqs.q: Is Ilam worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you like slow travel. Ilam is Nepal's main tea country, with garden walks, morning mist, cheap good tea and very few foreign tourists. It is not a trekking hub or a heritage town. Two or three nights here, with a day at Kanyam and one at Mai Pokhari, is a calm counterweight to Kathmandu and the big treks.

faqs.q: How do I get from Kathmandu to Ilam?
faqs.a: The quickest way is a 45–50 minute flight from Kathmandu to Bhadrapur, then about 100 km and 3–4 hours by car up the Mechi Highway. By road, overnight buses take 14–16 hours. A private car is best split over two days. Check current status of flights and roads before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Ilam?
faqs.a: October to December gives the clearest views and fresh autumn tea. March to May brings first and second flush plucking and rhododendrons on the higher ridges, with more haze. June to September is monsoon: green and quiet, but leeches, landslides and cloud. January and February are cold but often clear.

faqs.q: How many days do I need in Ilam?
faqs.a: Two nights covers Ilam Tea Estate, the bazaar and a half-day trip to Kanyam. Three nights adds Mai Pokhari or a homestay night in a farm village. If you want to reach Sandakpur for the Kanchenjunga and Everest view, plan four to five nights in the Ilam area.

faqs.q: Can I see Mount Everest from Ilam?
faqs.a: Not from Ilam bazaar. On clear days you see the Kanchenjunga range to the north from ridges above town. For Everest, Lhotse, Makalu and Kanchenjunga together you need to go up to Sandakpur, on the Singalila ridge at 3,636 m, a long jeep day north of Ilam.

faqs.q: Is Ilam safe for tourists?
faqs.a: Ilam is a quiet, friendly hill town and we consider it safe for travellers, including solo women. The main risks are road ones: narrow hill roads, monsoon landslides and night driving. We avoid driving after dark and plan around the weather. Usual sense with valuables applies in buses and bazaars.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Ilam?
faqs.a: No special permit is needed for Ilam town, the tea gardens or Kanyam. Ilam is not a restricted area. A small local fee is sometimes collected at sites such as Mai Pokhari. Carry your passport, as some hotels and checkposts record foreign guests.

faqs.q: What food is Ilam known for?
faqs.a: Ilam is known for its tea, the small round akabare chilli, milk and dairy products including chhurpi cheese, cardamom and ginger. Try akabare achar with dal bhat in the bazaar, and buy orthodox tea by weight from the shops on the main road.

faqs.q: Where should I stay in Ilam?
faqs.a: Stay in the bazaar close to Ilam Tea Estate so you can walk into the gardens at dawn. Choose from simple hotels and family guesthouses there, or spend a night in a village homestay outside town. There are no large resort hotels; comfort is basic but clean.
